name: Jenkins
summary: The self-hosted automation server much of CI started on: a Java controller that hands jobs to agents, more than 2,300 plugins, and pipelines written as a `Jenkinsfile`.
intro: Jenkins is a Java web application you run yourself. The controller serves the web UI, schedules work and keeps everything as files under `$JENKINS_HOME`: its configuration, the job definitions, every build record and the plugins. Builds run on agents, other machines or containers connected to the controller. The docs advise against running builds on the controller’s own built-in node, because a build there has the same access to the controller’s files as Jenkins itself. Nearly everything beyond scheduling comes from plugins, for source control, credentials, cloud agents, test reports and notifications; the plugin index lists more than 2,300.

Since Jenkins 2.0 in April 2016, the usual way to describe a build is Pipeline: a `Jenkinsfile` committed to the repository, written in a Groovy-based syntax, either the stricter Declarative form or the free-form Scripted one. It splits the work into stages of steps such as `sh 'make'`, can build every branch and pull request, and survives restarts of the controller. The Configuration as Code plugin does the same for the controller, setting it up from a YAML file instead of the web UI. Jenkins ships weekly releases and long-term support (LTS) lines; the latest LTS, 2.580.2, came out on October 28, 2026 and needs Java 21 or 25. It was a founding project of the Continuous Delivery Foundation in 2019 and its first to graduate, in August 2020.
strengths: Runs on your own hardware, under the MIT licence, with no per-minute billing or vendor service in the path
A plugin for almost any tool, cloud or version control system, so it fits into whatever a company already runs
Pipelines live in a `Jenkinsfile` next to the code, are reviewed like code, and keep running across controller restarts
Two decades of production use and neutral governance at the Continuous Delivery Foundation
limits: You run it: the controller’s state is a directory of files to back up, and core and plugins need regular updates
Plugins are most of the attack surface: seven of the ten security advisories Jenkins published in 2026 up to October 28 involved plugins
Pipeline Groovy always runs on the controller, using its CPU and memory; the docs say to keep logic in `sh` steps that run on agents
Upgrades follow Java: since 2.555.1 Jenkins needs Java 21 or 25, and the last LTS line to support Java 17 ended in March 2026

story: Kohsuke Kawaguchi, an engineer at Sun Microsystems, started Hudson in the summer of 2004 and released it in February 2005. It built and tested projects on every change, and its plugin system let other developers add support for their own tools.

After Oracle bought Sun in 2010, the community and Oracle disagreed over the project’s infrastructure and its name, which Oracle had applied to register as a trademark. In January 2011 Andrew Bayer wrote that without a binding guarantee the project would be “living under a sword of Damocles”, and the community voted to rename it Jenkins, with Kawaguchi registering the new trademark to hand to a non-profit. Oracle kept developing Hudson, gave it to the Eclipse Foundation at the end of 2012, and it was declared obsolete in 2017.

Jenkins 2.0, announced on April 26, 2016, put Pipeline as code at the centre: build definitions moved from forms in the web UI into a `Jenkinsfile` in the repository. In 2019 Jenkins became one of four founding projects of the Continuous Delivery Foundation, and in August 2020 its first graduated project. It has kept its weekly and LTS release lines since, moving to Java 21 as the minimum in 2026.

choices.choice: A small core and everything else as plugins
choices.why: Every team used a different mix of version control, build tools and test reports. Plugins let the community add support for each without changing the core, and the index has grown past 2,300.

choices.choice: A controller that hands builds to agents
choices.why: Spreading builds over many machines adds capacity and lets each build run on the operating system it needs; it also keeps untrusted build scripts away from the controller’s files.

choices.choice: Rename rather than live with Oracle’s trademark
choices.why: Oracle could withdraw the right to use “Hudson” at any time, so the community chose a new name it controlled instead.

choices.choice: Pipelines as code in a Groovy-based language
choices.why: Jobs configured by clicking couldn’t be versioned or reviewed. A `Jenkinsfile` checked in with the source is versioned with it, and a Groovy-based language keeps complex pipelines manageable.
